Non-optical and nonlinear properties
-------------------------------------

Every material carries these properties, read back with ``get('<material>')`` and
used by ``heat()``, ``electrostatic()``, and the chi(2) EME. ``dn_dT`` and ``eps_r_dc``
are one value for every axis, or three for the crystal's x, y and z principal axes,
which turn with the material like its index. KTP and LBO store ``dn_dT`` for all three
axes. Uniaxial crystals store the optic-axis (extraordinary) value of ``dn_dT`` and
``eps_r_dc`` as one value, and so does KTP for ``eps_r_dc``. ``d`` (chi(2)) and ``r``
(the linear electro-optic, or Pockels, tensor) are both contracted coefficients in the
crystal frame (pm/V). Only the nonzero independent coefficients are listed, and ``0``
means all coefficients are zero (or, for ``r``, not applicable, as for a material with no
``r`` method). A
thermal conductivity of ``1e-10``, a ``dn_dT`` of ``0``, or a resistivity of ``inf`` is
the database default, used where no reliable published value exists. Every non-default
value has a citation in the material's ``property_refs`` dict
(``get('<material>')['property_refs']``). Consult the source code in ``EMP_materials.py``
for the full citation text.

Not available (default values used):

* ``dn_dT`` for HfO2, TiO2, TiO2_rutile, GaP, GaSb, InAs, InSb, InGaAs, InGaP, AlGaAs,
  and GGG.
* ``d`` for InP.

``r`` is currently only entered for LN, LN_MgO, GaAs, InP, AlN, GaN, and KTP, the
materials the electrostatic phase-shifter example uses. Every other material's ``r`` is
the base-class zero tensor.

Optimization
------------

:data:`optimize` finds the parameters of a simulation you have already set up that give the best value of a quantity you choose, within bounds and constraints (EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  only). The parameters are named with the keys of :data:`sweep`: a setting (``'wavelength'``), one profile's setting (``'setting, <profile>, <name>'``), a shape property (``'shape, <name>, <property>'``), a section property (``'section, <name>, <property>'``), or an argument of a :data:`monitor_coupling` beam (``'beam, <name>'``).

Every evaluation starts from the simulation as declared when :data:`optimize` is called. It sets each parameter, solves what the objectives need (a mode solve for a mode quantity, :data:`EME` for an S-matrix or a monitor coupling) and records the result, so an evaluation depends only on its parameters, whatever ran before it. A cross-section that an earlier evaluation solved is not solved again: optimizing a section length solves the modes once, and optimizing a beam's angle on a solved chain solves nothing. At the end, the simulation is left solved at the best point, so :data:`get`, :data:`plot` and :data:`EME` read it.

The objectives and constraints are declared as data with the classes below, imported from ``emodeconnection``:

.. code-block:: python

    from emodeconnection import Parameter, Objective, Constraint

    res = em.optimize(
        parameters=[Parameter('section, coupler, length', bounds=(5e3, 40e3), x0=15e3)],
        objective=Objective('S_power', out='coupler.out_right', into='coupler.in_left'),
        constraints=[Constraint('section, coupler, length', '<=', 30e3)],
    )
    print(res.parameters, res.objective, res.status)

.. data:: optimize

    Find the parameters that give the best objective, within bounds and constraints.

    :param parameters: what to vary, a ``Parameter`` or a list of them
    :param objective: what to improve, an ``Objective`` or a list of them, whose weighted sum is improved
    :param constraints: limits on a parameter or on an objective's quantity, a ``Constraint`` or a list of them, default: None
    :param str method: 'cobyqa' (bounds and constraints, no derivatives), 'nelder-mead' or 'powell' (bounds, constraints by a penalty), 'differential_evolution' (a global search over finite bounds, constraints too), 'l-bfgs-b' (bounds, with a gradient) or 'slsqp' (bounds and constraints, with a gradient), default: 'cobyqa'
    :param gradient: how 'l-bfgs-b' and 'slsqp' get a gradient: 'finite_difference' evaluates the point and one step in each parameter, default: None (the pulsed adjoint for a poling design with pulse objectives, finite differences otherwise)
    :type gradient: str or None
    :param int max_evaluations: the most evaluations to make, default: 100
    :param max_time: [s] the most time to run, default: None (no limit)
    :type max_time: float or None
    :param float tolerance: the convergence tolerance, relative to each parameter's range, default: 1e-4
    :param int seed: the random seed of 'differential_evolution', so a run can be repeated, default: 0
    :param bool apply_best: leave the simulation solved at the best point, default: True
    :param record: a file to write each evaluation to as one line of JSON as it completes, so an interrupted run keeps its history, default: None
    :type record: str or None
    :param snapshot: also write the starting point to this ``.eph`` file, which :data:`evaluate` can evaluate from in another session, default: None
    :type snapshot: str or None
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    Returns an ``OptimizationResult``.

    A constraint on a parameter (``'<='`` or ``'>='``) narrows that parameter's bounds, so it is met exactly. A constraint on an objective's quantity is met to the method's tolerance. Each method spends evaluations differently: 'cobyqa' needs a few evaluations per parameter per step, finite differences one more evaluation than there are parameters per gradient, and 'differential_evolution' fifteen per parameter per generation. The result of a mode solve reproduces to about 1e-9 on the same grid, so set ``tolerance`` above that for objectives read from a mode solve.

.. class:: Parameter(key, bounds=None, x0=None, shape=(), step=None)

    A quantity to vary.

    :param str key: the parameter, as a :data:`sweep` key, ``'beam, <name>'`` (one of 'angle', 'mode_field_diameter', 'center', 'index' and 'polarization'), or ``'poling, <section>, domain_lengths'``, the length [nm] of every domain of a section with a ``PulsedProcess`` (``'poling, <section>, domain_lengths[k]'`` for domain k alone)
    :param bounds: (min, max), either end None for no limit, default: None
    :param x0: the starting value, default: None (the value the simulation holds now, or for a beam argument the value in the objective's ``beam``)
    :type x0: float or None
    :param step: the finite-difference step as a fraction of the bounded range (or of the value when unbounded), default: None (1e-6)
    :type step: float or None

    :param shape: the shape of a list of values, such as ``(n,)``, for ``'poling, <section>, domain_lengths'``, default: () (one value, or for the domain lengths the number of domains the section holds now)
    :type shape: tuple

    A shape's ``'position'`` given one value moves the shape in x and keeps its height. ``bounds`` of a list of values is one ``(min, max)`` for every element, or a list of them, one per element.

**Poling design.** Every domain of a poled section can be a free variable. ``Parameter('poling, <section>, domain_lengths', bounds=(1500, 6000))`` varies the length of each domain within a fabrication minimum and maximum, starting from the section's declared poling as domains (``Poling.to_domain_lengths``). ``'poling, <section>, total_length'``, the sum of the domain lengths, can be constrained (``Constraint('poling, ppln, total_length', '<=', 5e6)``), which costs no evaluation. Each evaluation propagates the pulse through the chain the last :data:`EME` prepared, with new domain walls, and solves no mode. With 'l-bfgs-b' or 'slsqp' and ``'band_energy'`` or ``'band_average'`` objectives, the gradient with respect to every domain comes from one adjoint propagation, so one evaluation with its gradient costs one and a half to two and a half propagations, whatever the number of domains. With ``gradient='finite_difference'`` a gradient costs one propagation per domain, which suits tens of domains but not thousands.

.. class:: Objective(kind, goal='maximize', target=None, weight=1.0, ...)

    A quantity to improve. ``kind`` and the arguments that select it:

    * ``'S_power'`` and ``'S_phase'``: :math:`|S|^2` and the phase of one S-matrix element. ``out`` and ``into`` name the ports, by name (its mode 0), as ``'<port>_<mode>'``, or as a mode index of the whole matrix, and ``wavelength`` picks one wavelength of a multi-wavelength circuit.
    * ``'monitor_coupling'``: :data:`monitor_coupling` of the monitor ``monitor`` for the beam ``beam``, a dict of that function's arguments.
    * ``'effective_index'``, ``'group_index'`` and ``'loss'`` (dB/m): of mode ``mode`` (default 0) of ``profile`` (default the default profile).
    * ``'band_energy'`` (pJ) and ``'band_average'`` (average power, W): of a pulse after pulsed propagation, between the wavelengths ``band = (min, max)`` in nm, for tracked mode ``mode`` (default all of them).
    * ``'parameter'``: the value of the parameter ``key`` itself, to make a device as short or as narrow as its constraints allow.

    :param str goal: 'maximize', 'minimize', or 'target', which minimizes the squared distance to ``target``, default: 'maximize'
    :param target: the value to reach with ``goal='target'``, default: None
    :type target: float or None
    :param float weight: the objective's weight in a list of them, default: 1.0

    ``value(results)`` returns the objective's quantity from an evaluation's results.

.. class:: Constraint(quantity, op, value)

    A limit.

    :param quantity: a parameter key, or an ``Objective`` whose quantity is limited
    :type quantity: str or Objective
    :param str op: '<=', '>=' or '=='
    :param float value: the limit

.. class:: OptimizationResult

    What :data:`optimize` returns. ``parameters`` is the best point by key and ``x`` the same as a list, ``objective`` and ``constraints`` its values, and ``goal`` says whether the objective was maximized or minimized. With several objectives that are not all maximized, ``objective`` is the minimized sum of each one's value (minimized), negative value (maximized) or squared distance from its target, each times its weight. ``status`` is 'converged', 'budget' (``max_evaluations`` ran out), 'time' (``max_time`` ran out) or 'failed', and ``message`` says more. ``history`` lists every evaluation as an ``Evaluation`` with its ``index``, ``parameters``, ``objective``, ``constraints``, the ``results`` the objectives read, ``seconds``, ``solves`` (the mode solves it made), ``cache_hits`` (the solves and junctions it reused) and ``cached`` (a point the run had already evaluated, which costs nothing). ``best`` is the best evaluation, ``evaluations`` the number actually solved and ``seconds`` the run's time. ``to_json()`` gives the whole result as plain JSON-ready data.

.. data:: evaluate

    Evaluate the simulation at one point. It starts from the simulation's snapshot (:data:`snapshot`, or the simulation as it was at the first evaluation), sets every parameter, solves what the results need and returns a record. The same parameters give the same results whatever ran before. Available in every session.

    :param dict parameters: {key: value} for every parameter, with the keys of :data:`optimize`
    :param results: the quantities to return, any :data:`get` key, 'S_matrix' or 'monitor_coupling', default: 'effective_index'
    :type results: str or list
    :param snapshot: a snapshot file to evaluate from instead of this simulation's snapshot, default: None
    :type snapshot: str or None
    :param monitor: the monitor of a 'monitor_coupling' result, default: None
    :type monitor: str or None
    :param beam: the arguments of :data:`monitor_coupling` for a 'monitor_coupling' result, default: None
    :type beam: dict or None
    :param profile: the profile a mode result is read from, default: None (the default profile)
    :type profile: str or None
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    Returns a dict with ``parameters``, ``results``, ``seconds``, ``solves``, ``cache_hits`` and ``seeded``.

.. data:: snapshot

    Take the snapshot :data:`evaluate` starts from: the simulation as declared now (profiles, shapes, sections, ports and settings), without anything solved. Available in every session.

    :param file_name: also write the snapshot to this ``.eph`` file, which another session can :data:`evaluate` from, default: None
    :type file_name: str or None
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    Returns the file's path when ``file_name`` is given.



Simulation setup
----------------

.. _coordinate-system:

.. rubric:: Coordinate system

A profile's cross-section lies in the x-y plane, in nm. The origin (x = 0, y = 0) is at the horizontal center of the simulation window's south (bottom) boundary. x runs from -``window_width``/2 to ``window_width``/2, with east at +x, and y runs from 0 to ``window_height``, with north up. A shape's ``position`` is its center in these coordinates and defaults to (0, 'auto'). An 'auto' y stacks the layer on top of the previous one, and the first such layer is the substrate, which rests on y = 0 and continues downward without bound.

A port's ``window`` and a section's ``offset`` are placed by their origin, the horizontal center and bottom edge of the window, displaced by ``offset = (dx, dy)`` from the section's own origin. Connecting two ports makes their origins coincide (see :data:`connect_ports`).

Sections are laid out along the EME propagation axis z. The first section declared starts at the origin and defines the global frame, and each connection places the next section where its port meets the one before. Along a section, w is the distance along its own path and x is across it in the section's own frame, so after a bend the section's x turns with it. ``plot(view='layout')`` draws the z-x panel in these chip coordinates, both in μm, with x increasing downward.

.. figure:: https://docs.emodephotonix.com/_images/coordinate_system.png
    :width: 100%

    Left, a cross-section: the window, a shape at ``position = (0, 1000)`` on an automatically stacked substrate, and a port window whose origin is offset by (700, 250). Right, a straight section and a 90° bend on the chip, as ``plot(view='layout')`` draws them.

.. data:: settings

    Specify the simulation settings.

    :param str profile: name of the profile these settings apply to, default: '_default'
    :param float wavelength: [nm] simulation wavelength, or a list of wavelengths for a multi-wavelength profile that ``FDM()``, ``FEM()``, ``solve()`` and ``EME()`` solve at each one. Setting a new wavelength on a multi-wavelength profile starts it over at that wavelength, default: 1550
    :param float frequency: [Hz] simulation frequency (an alternative to setting the wavelength), default: None
    :param excitation: declare a CW pump driving the circuit (EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  only), as ``Source(port=..., wavelength=..., mode=0, power=1.0, phase=0.0)`` from ``emodeconnection``, where ``power`` is in W and ``phase`` in radians. ``port`` is a bare side ('left'/'right') or a qualified '<section>.<port>' name, resolved when the circuit is built, and ``wavelength`` [nm] is matched against the circuit's own wavelengths. This is what makes :data:`EME` solve the power-dependent response of a :math:`\chi^{(2)}` section in addition to the small-signal scattering matrix. The result is read back with ``get('response')``, and the declared source with ``get('sources')``. A ``PulsedSource`` instead launches a femtosecond pulse for the pulsed nonlinear solver, see :ref:`pulsed nonlinear propagation <pulsed-propagation>`. Default: None
    :type excitation: Source or PulsedSource or None
    :param float x_resolution: [nm] resolution in the x-direction, default: 10
    :param float y_resolution: [nm] resolution in the y-direction, default: 10
    :param float window_width: [nm] simulation window width
    :param float window_height: [nm] simulation window height
    :param boundary_condition: the boundary condition as two characters 'XX', the first for the south wall and the second for the west wall (see the :ref:`coordinate system <coordinate-system>`). '0' is a metal wall with no symmetry, 'S' a symmetry wall where Ex is symmetric and 'A' one where it is anti-symmetric. 'TE' and 'TM' fold the window about every middle the structure is mirror symmetric about, to find the TE and TM modes. 'TE-h' and 'TM-h' fold only about the vertical middle (x = 0, left-right symmetry), 'TE-v' and 'TM-v' only about the horizontal middle (y = ``window_height`` / 2, top-bottom symmetry). Symmetry is a property of the whole cross-section, the material at every point of the window: two cores mirrored about the middle fold, and a shape made of the background material (a SiO2 BOX in a SiO2 background) does not break a fold. A fold the structure does not allow is not applied: 'TE-h', 'TE-v', 'TM-h' and 'TM-v' warn and solve the full window, and 'TE' and 'TM' warn when the structure has no symmetry at all. An explicit 'S' or 'A' wall is always applied, with a warning when the structure is not symmetric about it, since the solve is then of the mirrored half. In an EME, a fold applies only when every section of the device is symmetric about it (see :data:`EME`). With an (anti-)symmetric wall, the ``pml_NSEW_bool`` setting is copied from the north/east perimeter to the south/west perimeter, default: '00'
    :type boundary_condition: str, length = 2
    :param int num_modes: number of modes to solve for, default: 1
    :param str field_to_solve: either 'Et' or 'Ht' to specify whether the transverse electric field or magnetic field is solved, default: 'Et'
    :param float max_effective_index: maximum value for the effective refractive index, if ``max_effective_index`` is 0 the maximum refractive index found in the simulation window is used, default: 0
    :param float tolerance: eigenmode solver convergence tolerance, if ``tolerance`` = 0 the computer's precision is used, default: 1e-12
    :param int solver_threads: maximum number of threads the sparse solver uses to factor this profile's systems, where 0 lets the solver choose (up to every core), default: 0
    :param str sparse_solver: sparse direct solver for this profile's solves, one of ``'auto'``, ``'rslab'`` or ``'pardiso'``, where ``'auto'`` uses MKL PARDISO on the x86 installers (Linux, Windows and Intel Mac) and rslab on the Apple silicon installer, and ``'pardiso'`` is available only in the x86 installers, default: 'auto'
    :param str solver: the mode solver used by ``solve()``, ``EME()`` and ``sweep()``: 'FDM' (finite difference), 'FEM' (finite element, EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  only), or 'default', which is the FDM in every session (the FEM runs only when asked for). Calling ``FDM()`` or ``FEM()`` sets this to that solver, default: 'default'
    :param int fem_order: (FEM) element order, 1 or 2. Order 2 converges much faster for the same mesh, default: 2
    :param float fem_points_per_wavelength: (FEM) mesh points per wavelength in each material before refinement, default: 4
    :param float fem_min_angle: [degrees] (FEM) smallest triangle angle allowed in the mesh, at most 34, default: 30
    :param float fem_refine_fraction: (FEM) fraction of the estimated error that each refinement step targets, marking the fewest triangles that carry it, default: 0.5
    :param int fem_max_refinements: (FEM) most adaptive refinement steps after the first solve, 0 disables refinement, default: 2
    :param float fem_neff_tolerance: (FEM) refinement stops once no requested mode's effective index changes by more than this relative amount, default: 1e-6
    :param int fem_max_dofs: (FEM) refinement stops before a mesh would exceed this many unknowns, default: 2000000
    :param float fem_mesh_wavelength: [nm] (FEM) build and refine the mesh at this wavelength and solve every wavelength on it, so the results of a wavelength scan change smoothly with wavelength. 0 meshes each solve at its own wavelength. ``sweep()`` over wavelength, a wavelength list and a pulsed simulation set it to their shortest wavelength when it is 0, default: 0
    :param float bend_radius: [nm] waveguide bend radius relative to the center of the window, must be positive and larger than window_width/2, if ``bend_radius`` = 0 no bending is used in the calculation, default: 0
    :param str bend_method: how a nonzero ``bend_radius`` is solved, either 'cylindrical' (the bend factor 1 + x/R added to the mode solver) or 'TO' (the straight cross-section solved with its material transformed by the bend's conformal map, transformation optics). Both work with the FDM and the FEM, in 2D and 3D sessions, and their effective indices differ by about 6e-4 at R = 10 um. With a PML, set ``max_effective_index`` just above the guided mode, since a TO bend's spectrum starts with PML modes. ``report()`` names the method next to the solver, and the 'Bend Mode Solvers' example compares the two, default: 'cylindrical'
    :param pml_NSEW_bool: indicates whether to use a pml on each of the 4 boundaries, [north, south, east, west], 0: no pml, 1: use pml, default: [0,0,0,0]
    :type pml_NSEW_bool: list, length = 4
    :param num_pml_layers: number of pml layers to use, either a single value that is applied to all boundaries or a list of 4 values, [north, south, east, west]. The FDM's pml is this many grid cells thick on a boundary whose ``pml_thickness`` is 0. The FEM has no grid cells, so for the FEM it refines the pml's mesh instead, and it does not set the pml's thickness. The default 10 meshes the pml at its material's resolution, 20 meshes it twice as finely and 5 half as finely. Setting it alone resets ``pml_thickness`` to 0, default: 10
    :type num_pml_layers: int or list with length = 4
    :param pml_thickness: [nm] pml thickness, either a single value that is applied to all boundaries or a list of 4 values, [north, south, east, west]. This is the delivered thickness, the real extent of the pml's stretched coordinate from the simulation window edge out to the outer pml wall, so it stays fixed when the resolution changes. That is what a grid convergence sweep needs, since ``num_pml_layers`` counts cells and so shrinks the absorber as the mesh is refined. In the FDM, a value of 0 on a boundary falls back to ``num_pml_layers`` there, so the two settings can be mixed per boundary. Because the delivered thickness is the integral of the ``pml_kappa_max``/``pml_order`` grading over the layer stack, the number of layers it resolves to depends on those two settings. It is also quantized to a whole number of layers, and a request that does not land on one is rounded with a warning stating what was delivered. The FEM delivers exactly the thickness asked for, and on a boundary where it is 0 the FEM chooses a thickness of twice the pml's imaginary depth :math:`\ln(1/R) / 2 k_0`, which ``pml_reflection`` (:math:`R`) and the wavelength set. With the default ``pml_reflection`` that is 2.87 um at 980 nm and 4.54 um at 1550 nm. An FEM pml thinner than that depth warns, since the pml's own modes then rise above the cladding index, where they can hide the guided modes. If both ``pml_thickness`` and ``num_pml_layers`` are given in the same ``settings()`` call, ``pml_thickness`` takes precedence. Otherwise whichever of the two was set most recently applies, default: 0
    :type pml_thickness: float or list with length = 4
    :param float pml_order: polynomial grading exponent of the pml stretch profile, default: 3
    :param float pml_reflection: the target round-trip reflection that the pml is designed for, which sets the maximum pml conductivity. Must be greater than 0 and less than 1, default: 1e-8
    :param float pml_kappa_max: the maximum real coordinate stretch, reached at the outer pml face. Both solvers grade the stretch as 1 + (``pml_kappa_max`` - 1) u\ :sup:`pml_order` across the pml, from u = 0 at its inner face to 1 at its outer face, so for a given ``pml_thickness`` a larger value makes the pml's footprint thinner by the factor 1 + (``pml_kappa_max`` - 1) / (``pml_order`` + 1), 2.5 at the defaults. It must be at least 1, default: 7
    :param float pml_alpha_max: the complex-frequency-shifted (CFS) pml term, where 0 disables it. Raise it if the solve returns too many artificial pml modes, where ``0.1*omega*eps_0`` is a reasonable starting point that is small enough to barely move the physical modes, default: 0
    :param bool remove_pml_modes_bool: automatically remove the artificial modes of the pml regions from the mode list, identified as modes carrying less than 75% of their power inside the simulation window, default: False
    :param bool pml_seed_bool: seed the pml eigensolve with the fundamental mode of the same structure solved without a pml, so the guided fundamental lands at mode 0 without a hand-tuned ``max_effective_index``. This costs one extra single-mode solve, default: False
    :param background_material: background material, either a material name (from the material database) or a ~MaterialProperties or ~MaterialSpec object, default: "Vacuum"
    :type background_material: str or ~MaterialProperties or ~MaterialSpec
    :param expansion_resolution: [nm] single value or list of 4 values for the stretched grid resolution (ordered [north, south, east, west]). The grid is gradually transitioned from res to ``expansion_resolution``, default: 20
    :type expansion_resolution: float or list
    :param expansion_size: [nm] single value or list of 4 values for the approximate stretched distance (ordered [north, south, east, west]), default: 0
    :type expansion_size: float or list
    :param bool subpixel_avg: whether to use sub-pixel averaging of the permittivity/permeability at shape boundaries for improved accuracy, default: True
    :param bool generate_chi2: whether to generate the second-order nonlinear susceptibility (chi2) tensor for the simulation window, default: False
    :param bool include_heat: whether to include heat-related material properties when meshing for FEM heat calculations, default: True
    :param bool include_scattering: compute the interfacial scattering loss of every shape with roughness after each solve of this profile, whether the solve comes from ``FDM()``, ``FEM()``, ``solve()``, ``EME()`` or ``sweep()``, the same as calling ``scattering()`` after each one. ``FDM(scattering=True)`` does this for a single solve. Default: False
    :param propagation_resolution: [nm] resolution in the z-direction for plotting EME propagation results, default: wavelength/10
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: add_material

    Add a custom material by specifying a wavelength dependent equation.

    :param str name: material name, this will override the built-in material name if an identical name is used. A variable ``user_material_[name]`` will be created
    :param str refractive_index_equation: refractive index equation to evaluate as a function of the wavelength parameter 'x', where imaginary numbers are specified with a preceding 'j'. Only the following characters are allowed in the equation string: "0123456789 x j . + - ^ * / ( ) [ ]". A list of three equations can also be specified for non-isotropic materials, like '[n_xx, n_yy, n_zz]'. The string must have less than 1000 characters
    :param str wavelength_unit: either 'nm' or 'um' to specify the unit for the wavelength parameter 'x', default: 'um'
    :param list wavelength_range: [um] list of the minimum and maximum wavelength recommended for the refractive index equation, default: [0.2, 2.0]
    :param str citation: reference displayed in material explorer for the custom material, default: 'User defined.'
    :param float loss: the loss of the material in 'dB/m', default: 0.
    :param float thermal_conductivity: [W/m·K] thermal conductivity of the material, default: 1e-10
    :param float resistivity: [Ohm-nm] resistivity of the material, default: infinity
    :param float dn_dT: [K^-1] change in refractive index per change in temperature, relative to 298 K, default: 0
    :param float eps_r_dc: [-] relative permittivity at ~1 kHz, default: 1.0
    :param d: second-order nonlinear susceptibility d-matrix with shape (3, 6). Use None for linear materials, default: None
    :type d: list (3x6) or None
    :param float phi: [rad] rotation of the crystal about z, applied last, default: 0
    :param float theta: [rad] rotation of the crystal about y, default: 0
    :param float psi: [rad] rotation of the crystal about its own z axis, applied first, default: 0. The three angles turn the crystal by R = Rz(phi) Ry(theta) Rz(psi), the same convention as :class:`MaterialSpec`
    :param dict property_refs: citation string per property name (``'d'``, ``'r'``, ``'thermal_conductivity'``, ``'dn_dT'``, ``'eps_r_dc'``, ``'resistivity'``), default: {}
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: import_database

    Import a custom material database by specifying custom materials in a text file.

    :param str filename: name of text file to be imported
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    Here is an example of several custom materials in the database text file to be imported. See the ``add_material`` function for parameter details. Each custom material must contain the ``name`` and ``refractive_index_equation``, separated by a new line. Comments can be added with '#' or '%'. A ``name = ...`` line starts a new record (the spaces around ``=`` are optional). A record with no ``refractive_index_equation`` raises an error and nothing in the file is imported. ``wavelength_range`` is always in um regardless of ``wavelength_unit``, and defaults to ``[0.2, 2.0]`` when omitted. ``citation`` may contain an ``=`` sign.

        | name = custom_name_1
        | refractive_index_equation = equation_1
        | wavelength_unit = um (optional)
        | wavelength_range = [0.2, 2.0] (optional)
        | citation = reference_1 (optional, default: "User defined by database import.")
        |
        | # comment about my custom_SiO2 material
        | name = custom_SiO2
        | refractive_index_equation = (1 + 0.696166/(1 - (0.0684043/x)^2) + 0.4079426/(1 - (0.1162414/x)^2) + 0.8974794/(1 - (9.896161/x)^2))^0.5
        | wavelength_unit = um
        | wavelength_range = [0.21, 6.7]
        | citation = '(1) I. H. Malitson, "Interspecimen comparison of the refractive index of fused silica," J. Opt. Soc. Am. 55, 1205 (1965). (2) C. Z. Tan, "Determination of refractive index of silica glass for infrared wavelengths by IR spectroscopy," J. Non-Cryst. Solids 223, 158 (1998).'
        |
        | % comment about my custom_name_3 material
        | name = custom_name_3
        | refractive_index_equation = equation_3
        | wavelength_unit = nm

.. data:: shape

    Create or update a shape with attributes. These parameters are saved with 'shape\_'+name+'/' preceding the attribute name. If a name is not given, a number will be allocated as the shape name.

    :param str profile: name of the profile to add the shape to, default: '_default'
    :param str name: shape name, default: an auto-generated number
    :param material: the material for this shape.  Takes a string reference to a material in the Material Database, or a ~MaterialSpec or ~MaterialProperties object. default: "Vacuum"
    :type material: ~MaterialSpec, ~MaterialProperties, or str

    A shape's relative permeability comes from its material, for example ``material=MaterialProperties(n=1.5, mu=2.0)``, and the permeability of an etched region from ``fill_material`` in the same way. ``shape()`` has no permeability argument of its own, and the older ``permeability`` and ``fill_permeability`` arguments raise an error that says so.

    :param float loss_dB_per_m: [dB/m] material propagation loss, if not set by the ``material`` parameter, default: 0
    :param vertices: list of N vertices that define a closed polygon, or a list of such vertex lists to define multiple disjoint polygons in one shape. If specified the shape is a polygon (``shape_type`` 'polygon') defined by ``vertices`` (``width``, ``height``, ``position``, ``mask``, ``etch``, ``fill`` are ignored), to disable ``vertices``, set ``vertices`` to 0, default: 0
    :type vertices: list (N,2), list of list (N,2), or int
    :param float width: shape width, if left unspecified the shape is unbounded in x, extending past both sides of the simulation window, default: None
    :param height: shape height, or 'full_height' for a shape that is unbounded upward, extending past the top of the simulation window. Nothing can be automatically stacked on top of a shape of unbounded height, default: 0
    :type height: float or str
    :param position: centered x and y positions relative to the shape width and height, if the y position is left unspecified then it is treated like a layer stacked on top of the previous layer, and the first such layer is the substrate, unbounded downward past the bottom of the simulation window (a shape with an explicit y position never is), if only a single value is provided it is assumed to be the x position and the y position is left unspecified, default: (0, 'auto')
    :type position: list, length = 2
    :param mask: mask width for etching, centered on x-position set by ``position`` and ``mask_offset``, or a list of arbitrary length to specify multiple mask regions in combination with a list of ``mask_offset`` values, default: ``width``
    :type mask: float or list
    :param mask_offset: the x-position offset for the ``mask`` parameter, or a list of arbitrary length to specify multiple mask regions in combination with a list of ``mask`` values, default: ``0``
    :type mask_offset: float or list
    :param tone: 'n'/'N' or 'p'/'P' to define the pattern tone as negative or positive for the ``mask`` parameter, default: ``n``
    :type tone: str
    :param float etch_depth: etch depth for a layer outside the mask region, thickness = ``height`` - ``etch_depth``. The default ``mask`` covers the full width of the layer, so nothing is etched unless a narrower ``mask`` is given, default: 0
    :param float sidewall_angle: etched sidewall angle in degrees, 0 is perfectly vertical, 90 is the maximum. It is only applied to etched features (``height``, ``mask``, and a nonzero ``etch_depth`` must all be specified for this parameter to have any effect), default: 0
    :param fill_material: the material for the fill for this shape.  Takes the same values as material, as well as "transparent_fill" (the default). "transparent_fill" results in the fill being the background.
    :type fill_material: ~MaterialSpec, ~MaterialProperties, or str
    :param correlation_length: interfacial roughness correlation length, a single value is applied to all interfaces, a list of 2 applies the first value to all vertical interfaces and the second value to all horizontal interfaces, and a list with one value per edge of the shape's outline applies each value to its edge, in the order of the outline's vertices (for a shape defined by ``vertices``, the order given), default: [0,0]
    :type correlation_length: float or list
    :param roughness_rms: interfacial roughness standard deviation in nm rms, a single value is applied to all interfaces, a list of 2 applies the first value to all vertical interfaces and the second value to all horizontal interfaces, and a list with one value per edge of the shape's outline applies each value to its edge, in the order of the outline's vertices (for a shape defined by ``vertices``, the order given), default: [0,0]
    :type roughness_rms: float or list
    :param str shape_type: set shape type as 'planar', 'conformal' (only uses ``name``, ``material``, ``height``, and ``priority``), 'polygon' (only uses ``name``, ``vertices``, ``material`` and ``priority``), or 'ellipse' (only uses ``name``, ``material``, ``width``, ``height``, ``position``, ``sidewall_angle`` (the angle of the ellipse), and ``priority``), default: 'planar'
    :param float priority: a number that signifies the order in which shapes will be drawn, a higher priority gets drawn over a lower number priority, default: auto-generated integer based on order called
    :param float fem_resolution: [nm] approximate resolution to target for triangular meshing used by FEM functions, default: 500
    :param float current: [A] current flowing through the cross-section of the shape, which can generate heat, default: 0
    :param float voltage: [V] voltage of the shape, None for floating, default: None
    :param bool heat_only: specifies a shape that will only be rendered when meshing for a heat calculation, default: False
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    .. note::
        Shapes are positioned in absolute coordinates, independent of the simulation window, so a shape may extend beyond the window and the window can be resized or offset without re-seating the geometry. A layer whose bottom edge rests on y = 0, the reference plane that the automatic stacking starts from, is treated as the substrate: its material continues downward without bound, so a window that extends below y = 0 resolves to that layer rather than to the background material.

.. data:: reset

    Clear simulation settings, shape definitions, or both, on one profile (the default profile unless ``profile`` is given).

    ``'shapes'`` removes every user-defined shape from the profile (the background remains) and discards its mesh, mode list, and analysis results. ``'settings'`` replaces the profile with a new one of the same name at the default settings, which also removes its shapes, and on the default profile also resets ``propagation_resolution``. ``'all'`` does both. Other profiles are not affected. Any other ``kind`` raises an error, as does a profile that does not exist or one member of a multi-wavelength profile (``'NAME.WAVELENGTH'``), whose members share their shapes.

    :param str kind: either 'shapes', 'settings', or 'all' to specify what data is cleared, default: 'shapes'
    :param str profile: name of the profile to reset, default: '_default'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'



Solver and analysis
-------------------

.. data:: solve

    Calculate the waveguide modes with the finite-difference (FDM) or the finite-element (FEM) solver. The fields, effective indices, losses and TE fractions are saved as described under ``FDM()``, whichever solver runs.

    :param str solver_method: 'FDM' or 'FEM' runs that solver, the same as calling ``FDM()`` or ``FEM()``, and sets the profile's ``solver`` setting to it. 'default' runs the solver the ``solver`` setting selects, without changing it. That setting is itself 'default' unless changed, which is the FDM in every session, default: 'default'
    :param profile: profile name to save the solved profile under, default: '_default'
    :type profile: str or int
    :param str section: name of an EME section to solve a slice from, instead of the profile's own settings/shapes, default: None
    :param float propagation_distance: [nm] where along ``section`` to take the cross-section, default: None
    :param bool include_heat: whether to include the temperature change from the most recent ``heat()`` solve, default: True
    :param bool include_static: whether to apply the electro-optic (Pockels) permittivity perturbation from the most recent ``electrostatic()`` solve, default: True
    :param bool verbose: print progress, default: True
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'
    :return: what ``FDM()`` or ``FEM()`` returns, for whichever solver ran.

    .. note::
        The FEM solver requires an EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  license, so ``solve()`` needs one whenever it runs the FEM: with ``solver_method='FEM'``, or with 'default' when the profile's ``solver`` setting is 'FEM'. See :data:`FEM` on the Multi-Physics page.

.. data:: FDM

    Calculate the waveguide modes using the finite difference method. Calling ``FDM()`` sets the profile's ``solver`` setting to 'FDM', so ``EME()`` and ``sweep()`` then use the FDM too. It automatically runs ``EM_mesh`` as needed (generating ``x``, ``y``, ``permittivity``, and ``permeability``). After solving the mode, the effective index (``effective_index``), mode propagation loss (``loss_dB_per_m``), and field components (``Fx``, ``Fy``, ``Ex``, ``Ey``, ``Ez``, ``Hx``, ``Hy``, ``Hz``, ``Sx``, ``Sy``, ``Sz``) are available, where the fields are normalized to the equation below.

    .. math::
        \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Re} \iint \left( \vec E \times \vec H^* \right) \! \cdot \! \hat{z} \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y = 1 \, \mathrm{W}

    It also calculates the TE fraction of each mode (``TE_fraction``) with the following equation, and it saves the indices of the TE and TM modes (``TE_indices`` and ``TM_indices``).

    .. math::
        \mathrm{{TE_fraction}} = \frac{\iint \left| \vec E_\mathrm{x} \right|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y}{\iint \left| \vec E_\mathrm{x} \right|^2 + \left| \vec E_\mathrm{y} \right|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y}

    A multi-wavelength profile (a wavelength list in ``settings()``, or a set from ``create_profile_set()``) is solved at each of its wavelengths, and is saved as one solved profile per wavelength, so ``get()`` returns a dict keyed by wavelength and ``plot()`` and ``EME()`` use the modes at each wavelength. ``FEM()`` and ``solve()`` do the same. The direct return value then holds every wavelength's result, keyed by wavelength (see below).

    :param profile: profile name to automatically create a profile after running ``FDM()``, default: '_default'
    :type profile: str or int
    :param str section: name of an EME section to solve a slice from, instead of the profile's own settings/shapes, default: None
    :param float propagation_distance: [nm] optional propagation distance used to compute an additional propagation phase/loss, default: None
    :param str mode_filter: choose to filter the mode list for propagation direction of 'forward', 'backward', or 'none'. It acts in the anisotropic solver only, since the isotropic solver returns forward modes by construction. It is saved in the profile's settings, so a later ``EME()`` or ``sweep()`` that solves this profile again uses it too. Default: 'forward'
    :param int fLanczos: size of the eigensolver's Krylov subspace as a multiple of the number of modes requested, at least 1. Raise it if the solve does not converge. It is saved in the profile's settings like ``mode_filter``. Default: 5
    :param str solve_type: either 'isotropic', 'anisotropic', or 'auto' to control whether anisotropic materials are solved with the full tensor or reduced to their isotropic diagonal, default: 'auto'
    :param bool include_heat: whether to include heat-related material properties when meshing, default: True
    :param bool include_static: whether to apply the electro-optic (Pockels) permittivity perturbation from the most recent ``electrostatic()`` solve, default: True
    :param bool scattering: whether to automatically calculate interfacial scattering loss for all shapes after solving. The ``include_scattering`` setting in :data:`settings` does the same for every solve of the profile. Default: False
    :param bool verbose: print progress, default: True
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

    .. note::
        The direct return value of this function (as called through ``emodeconnection``) is a dict with keys ``field`` (a Field object), ``n_eff_tilde``, ``TE_fraction``, ``TE_indices``, ``TM_indices`` and ``PML_indices``. For a multi-wavelength profile it is a ``WavelengthDict`` of these dicts, one per wavelength, indexable like a ``dict[float, dict]`` (``result[1550]['n_eff_tilde']``). The individual field components and derived quantities described above (``effective_index``, ``loss_dB_per_m``, ``Ex``/``Ey``/etc.) become available afterward from the saved profile via ``get()``/``get_fields()``, not as top-level keys of this return value.

.. data:: sweep

    This function sweeps a calculation as a function of any available setting, shape parameter, or section parameter (EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  only). Run a parameter sweep of ``key`` over defined ``values`` by solving ``solve_type`` for each value and saving a list of parameters defined by 'result' that correspond to the ``values``. After running a sweep, the data will be available from a parameter called ``sweep_data``, which includes all of the specified parameters of this funcion and the data specified by the ``result`` parameter. The ``result`` parameter can include any parameter that is listed in the ``inspect()`` output (after running the desired simulation). Additionally, the ``result`` parameter can include 'scattering_loss' (a sum of all scattering losses for each mode) or 'mode_order' (a list of mode indices used for tracking the order of the modes).

    :param str key: any settings, shape, or section parameter that will have its value changed in the sweep, directly specify the key for settings parameters, specify 'shape, SHAPE_NAME, SHAPE_KEY' to specify shape the SHAPE_KEY of SHAPE_NAME, specify 'section, SECTION_NAME, SECTION_KEY' to specify the SECTION_KEY of SECTION_NAME. The accepted section keys are 'length', 'num_modes', 'minimum_z_step', 'overlap_variation', 'z_slices', 'offset', 'window_width', 'window_height', and 'facet_angle' (the tilt [degrees] of an angled facet on that section, see :func:`make_angled_facet_port`). Any other section key raises an error naming it. A shape's ``etch_depth``, ``sidewall_angle`` and ``tone`` are swept as 'shape, SHAPE_NAME, etch_depth' and so on.
    :param values: the values that define the ``key`` during the sweep
    :type values: list or array
    :param str solve_type: either 'mesh', 'FDM', or 'EME' to specify which solver to run at each sweep step, where 'FDM' means a mode solve with the solver the ``solver`` setting selects (the FDM or the FEM), default: automatically chosen based on the ``key`` and ``result`` selection
    :param result: the parameters to save from each iteration of the sweep.  This can be any value in the eph file.  Internally, this calls ``get``, so if you can read the value with ``get`` you can collect it with ``sweep``. Additionally, 'scattering_loss', 'mode_order' and 'monitor_coupling' are accepted. 'monitor_coupling' collects :data:`monitor_coupling` for the monitor named by ``monitor`` and the beam described by ``beam``. With a ``key`` that is one of the beam's arguments ('angle', 'mode_field_diameter', 'center', 'index' or 'polarization') the solved chain is reused and only the overlap is evaluated at each value, with no solve, and ``sweep_data`` also carries ``power_through_plane`` and ``overlap``. Any other key needs ``solve_type='EME'`` and solves the chain at each value. default: 'effective_index'
    :type result: str or list
    :param bool seed: whether to seed each solve step with the previous step's mode list, default: True
    :param bool adaptive: only for a wavelength sweep. ``values`` keeps its meaning (the wavelengths you want results at), and ``adaptive`` changes only *where the solver runs*: modes are matched between neighboring solves through a phase-corrected overlap, and a bisection in wavelength places further solves until the mode list stops moving by more than ``tolerance``, or the gap reaches ``minimum_step``. The requested wavelengths are then filled in by interpolating the solved mode lists, which is much cheaper than solving every point when the modes vary smoothly. ``sweep_data`` additionally carries ``solved_wavelengths`` (where the solver actually ran) and ``unconverged`` (any stretch the sampler gave up on, reported rather than raised). Default: False
    :param float tolerance: with ``adaptive``, the largest mode-list change tolerated between adjacent solves, default: 1e-3
    :param float minimum_step: [nm] with ``adaptive``, the smallest wavelength gap the sampler will bisect into, default: the spacing of ``values``
    :param str method: either 'direct' or 'interpolated'. 'interpolated' is only for ``key='wavelength'`` with ``result='S_matrix'`` (EMode\ :sup:`3D`\  only): the circuit is solved and refined once at the current wavelength with :data:`EME`, every cross-section in it is solved at ``num_nodes`` wavelengths (Chebyshev-Lobatto nodes, ends included) over ``wavelength_range``, and the S-matrix at each of ``values`` is rebuilt from the propagation constants and junctions interpolated between them, so no wavelength in ``values`` solves anything. It suits the hundreds of wavelengths a resonator spectrum needs. A mode that cannot be followed across the range keeps its solve at the current wavelength (its effective index and its junction coupling) at every wavelength, with a warning naming its cross-sections, so the result at the current wavelength is always the solved circuit. One node is predicted from the others: ``sweep_data`` additionally carries ``num_nodes``, ``interpolation_residual`` (the largest error at that node in a slice's propagation phase factor or in a junction's S-matrix element) and ``interpolation_residuals`` (the node's wavelength, the slice and junction errors, and the largest error of the whole circuit's S-matrix). A warning naming the slice or junction is logged when ``interpolation_residual`` exceeds ``interpolation_tolerance``. The whole circuit's error is not checked, since a narrow resonance moved by a small fraction of its width changes it by order one. Default: 'direct'
    :param int num_nodes: with ``method='interpolated'``, the number of wavelengths every cross-section is solved at, at least 4. Add nodes, or narrow the range, when ``interpolation_residual`` is too large, default: 8
    :param wavelength_range: [nm] with ``method='interpolated'``, the range the nodes span, which must contain every one of ``values``, default: the range of ``values``
    :type wavelength_range: tuple[float, float]
    :param float interpolation_tolerance: with ``method='interpolated'``, the largest ``interpolation_residual`` accepted without a warning, default: 1e-4
    :param str monitor: with ``result='monitor_coupling'``, the name of the monitor (see :data:`monitor`), default: None
    :param dict beam: with ``result='monitor_coupling'``, the keyword arguments of :data:`monitor_coupling` that describe the beam, ``mode_field_diameter`` at least, for example ``beam=dict(mode_field_diameter=10.4e3)``. A beam ``key`` overrides its entry here at each value, default: None
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: converge

    Find the resolution, window, PML thickness or number of modes a result needs. ``converge()`` varies ``setting`` one step at a time, solving the profile at each step, and watches one quantity of one mode, the ``target``. It stops once the target has settled to within ``tolerance``, prints one row per solve and returns the history. The profile's settings change only with ``apply=True``, so the table can be read first. It runs in every license tier.

    Each setting is varied in its own way:

    * ``'resolution'``: ``x_resolution`` and ``y_resolution`` together, from 20 cells per wavelength in the highest-index material, finer by a factor of :math:`\sqrt{2}` a step. Each step is rounded down so a whole number of cells fills the window and, where the shapes allow, every shape edge lies on a grid line. With ``solver='FEM'`` it varies ``fem_points_per_wavelength`` from 1 in the same ratio, with ``fem_max_refinements=0`` so the routine and not the FEM's own refinement sets each step.
    * ``'window'``: ``window_width`` and ``window_height``, from the core (every shape bounded on all four sides) plus three decay lengths :math:`1 / (k_0 \sqrt{n_\mathrm{eff}^2 - n_\mathrm{clad}^2})` of the cladding, growing by one decay length on each side a step. The window stays centered on the core, and an axis folded by ``boundary_condition`` stays centered on its mirror plane. On a bend, the outer side starts beyond the caustic :math:`n_\mathrm{eff} R / n_\mathrm{clad}`.
    * ``'pml'``: ``pml_thickness`` on every side with a PML, from one wavelength in the cladding, growing by half a wavelength a step. With the FEM it starts no thinner than the PML's imaginary depth (see ``pml_thickness`` under :data:`settings`). It needs a PML (``pml_NSEW_bool``).
    * ``'modes'``: ``num_modes``, doubling until the watched mode is among the modes confined to the window rather than to the PML.
    * ``'all'``: the window on the coarsest grid, the PML (when one is on), the resolution, the number of modes, then one more check of the window at the final grid.

    The rule that stops it depends on how the setting converges. The resolution converges algebraically, so each step's error is estimated as :math:`|\Delta_k| / (r^p - 1)`, from the change :math:`\Delta_k` since the previous step, the refinement ratio :math:`r` and the order :math:`p` observed over the last three steps (between 1 and 4). A window and a PML converge exponentially, so the estimate is the change itself. The routine stops as ``'converged'`` once the estimated error is at or below the tolerance on two consecutive steps, and reports the last step's settings. A change that flips sign between two consecutive steps stops it as ``'oscillating'``, since a sequence that alternates has not converged whatever its size. The orthogonality target is the largest overlap between two modes (as :data:`orthogonality` computes it), which must fall below the tolerance rather than settle, and a run that stops improving it ends as ``'stalled'``. ``max_solves`` or ``max_time`` running out ends a run as ``'budget'``.

    The watched mode is followed from one step to the next by its overlap, not by its place in the mode list, so a PML mode that moves ahead of it does not change what is watched. A step with no mode overlapping the watched one above 0.9 stops the run as ``'lost mode'``. One mode of a degenerate pair (a round fiber, a square core) can come back in another polarization from one solve to the next, so fold such a window with ``boundary_condition`` before converging it.

    :param str setting: 'resolution', 'window', 'pml', 'modes' or 'all', default: 'resolution'
    :param str target: 'effective_index', 'group_index' (from :data:`group_index`), 'loss' (``loss_dB_per_m``, with the scattering loss when ``include_scattering`` is set) or 'orthogonality', default: 'effective_index'
    :param float tolerance: the largest acceptable estimated error, absolute for 'effective_index' (default 1e-4), 'group_index' (1e-3) and 'orthogonality' (1e-6), and relative for 'loss' (1e-2)
    :param bool apply: write the chosen settings to the profile, default: False
    :param int max_solves: the most solves to make, across every setting of 'all', default: 20
    :param float max_time: [s] the most time to take, default: None (no limit)
    :param int mode: the mode to watch, an index into the first solve's mode list, default: 0
    :param str profile: the profile to converge, default: '_default'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'
    :return: a ``ConvergenceResult`` with ``status``, ``chosen`` (the chosen settings, as :data:`settings` takes them), ``history`` (one row per solve: ``setting``, ``value``, ``settings``, ``quantity``, ``change``, ``estimated_error`` and ``seconds``), ``stages`` (one per setting varied, with its status, its chosen settings and, for the resolution, its observed ``order``) and ``seconds``. ``print(result)`` prints the table again. The same result is saved on the profile as ``convergence``.

    The guide of the :doc:`Straight Waveguide Convergence </examples/Straight_Convergence>` example, a 2000 x 200 nm SiN core in SiO2 at 980 nm, has a known effective index, 1.6874538. Converging its resolution to 1e-4:

    .. code-block:: python

        em.settings(wavelength=980, window_width=7000, window_height=4200, num_modes=1,
                    boundary_condition='TE', background_material='SiO2')
        em.shape(name='core', material='SiN', width=2000, height=200, position=[0, 2100])
        result = em.converge('resolution', 'effective_index', tolerance=1e-4)

    .. code-block:: text

        setting                   value         n_eff     change  est. error  time (s)
        resolution             23.81 nm      1.686959          -           -       1.5
        resolution             16.67 nm      1.687108    1.5e-04     4.8e-04       1.3
        resolution              11.9 nm      1.687301    1.9e-04     4.3e-04       3.1
        resolution             8.475 nm      1.687368    6.7e-05     4.1e-05       5.4

        resolution: converged (x_resolution=8.474576271186441, y_resolution=8.333333333333334, estimated error 4.1e-05, order 3.09)
        converged at 0.0001 absolute in 12.8 s

    The x resolutions divide the 500 nm lattice of the core's side walls and the y resolutions the 200 nm lattice of its top and bottom, so every edge lies on a grid line. The chosen 8.5 nm grid is 8.5e-5 from the reference, within the tolerance. ``em.converge('resolution', 'effective_index', tolerance=1e-4, apply=True)`` would also set ``x_resolution`` and ``y_resolution`` to those values.

.. data:: confinement

    Calculate confinement factor of specified shape. By default, only the area of the shape that is used to define the refractive index profile is included in the confinement factor. For instance, if another shape with a higher priority overlaps the specified shape, the overlapped area is not included. The confinement factors are also returned by this function. For a multi-wavelength profile, the return value is a dict keyed by wavelength.

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param shape_list: name (from ``shape``) or list of names of shapes to include in confinement or 'all' for all shapes, default: 'all'
    :type shapes: str or list
    :param mode_list: desired modes to calculate confinement, 'all', 'TE', 'TM', or a list of the desired mode indices, default: 'all'
    :type mode_list: str or list
    :param vertices: list of vertices that define a closed polygon, specifying this parameter will override the ``shape_list`` input, default: None
    :type vertices: list (Nx2)
    :param bool ignore_priority: toggle ignoring overlapped shapes with higher priority, default: False
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: effective_area

    Calculate the effective areas for all modes. After running this function, an array called ``effective_area`` will become available and ``report`` will display the effective areas. The ``effective_area`` is also returned by this function and is in units of :math:`\mu\text{m}^2`. For a multi-wavelength profile, the return value is a dict keyed by wavelength.

    .. math::
        A_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\left( \iint \left| \vec E \right|^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \right)^2}{\iint \left| \vec E \right|^4 \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y} \, \mu\text{m}^2

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: orthogonality

    Calculate the highest value of mode overlap between modes in the mode list. After running this function, a variable called ``maximum_overlap`` will become available in metadata of the named (or default) profile, and the ``maximum_overlap`` is returned by this function. For a multi-wavelength profile, the return value is a dict keyed by wavelength. Ideally, this value is less than :math:`10^{-3}`, indicating an accurate mode list.

    :param profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :type profile: str or int
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: group_index

    Calculate the group index for all modes. First, ``group_index`` runs ``FDM`` (if not already run), then it runs ``FDM`` a second time with 0.01 % longer wavelength to calculate the group index. After running this function, an array called ``group_index`` will become available and ``report`` will display the group index. The ``group_index`` array is also returned by this function. For a multi-wavelength profile, the return value is a dict keyed by wavelength.

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: report

    Display a simulation report table with information about each mode:

    - mode number
    - effective index
    - TE fraction
    - loss (dB/m)
    - a ``PML`` column when the profile was solved with a PML, marking the modes that carry less than 75% of their power inside the window (see ``PML_indices`` and ``window_confinement`` in :doc:`Variable Descriptions </emodeguide/variables>`)
    - per-shape confinement factors and scattering loss (if calculated)
    - effective areas (if calculated)

    The line above the table gives the wavelength and the mode solver that produced the modes, for example ``Wavelength: 1550.0 nm    Solver: FEM``. A saved CSV records both below the table.

    Returns the table as a dictionary keyed by profile name, each table holding one list per column. A multi-wavelength profile returns one table per wavelength, keyed by wavelength. An unsolved profile returns an empty table.

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param bool save: whether to save the table to a file or not, default: False
    :param str file_name: name of the file to save, default: 'mode_report'
    :param str file_type: file type to save, 'txt', 'latex', or 'csv', default: 'txt'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: label_profile

    Saves a copy of the default profile (settings, shapes, mesh and any solved modes) under ``name`` in the ``profiles`` dictionary of the simulation file, meshing it first if needed. A multi-wavelength profile is saved whole, with each member meshed and keeping its own name. Named profiles are read with ``profile=NAME`` in :data:`get`, :data:`get_fields`, :data:`get_grid`, :data:`get_shape` and :data:`get_profile`, and one wavelength of a multi-wavelength one with ``profile='NAME.WAVELENGTH'``. They are the inputs to ``overlap``, ``mode_order`` and the EME section functions, and :data:`reset` changes one only when given its name.

    :param str name: save the current simulation state to this name, default: '0'
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: overlap

    Calculate overlap integral between two modes. The result is returned by this function and saved on the profile named by ``profile_b``, where ``get('overlap', profile=profile_b)`` reads the latest result and ``get('overlaps', profile=profile_b)`` a record of every overlap computed against it (see :doc:`Variable Descriptions </emodeguide/variables>`).

        Coldren, Larry A., Scott W. Corzine, and Milan L. Mashanovitch, ''Diode lasers and photonic integrated circuits,'' John Wiley \& Sons, 2012.

    .. math::
        \mathrm{overlap} = \frac{4 n_\mathrm{eff,1} n_\mathrm{eff,2}}{(n_\mathrm{eff,1} + n_\mathrm{eff,2})^2} \frac{\left| \iint \vec E_1 \times \vec H_2 \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \right|^2}{\iint \left| \vec E_1 \times \vec H_1 \right| \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y \, \iint \left| \vec E_2 \times \vec H_2 \right| \, \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}y}

    :param profile_a: label of first profile, default: '_default'
    :type profile_a: str or int
    :param int mode_a: mode number from the first profile, default: 0
    :param str simulation_name_a: simulation name for the first mode set, default: 'emode'
    :param profile_b: label of second profile, default: '_default'
    :type profile_b: str or int
    :param int mode_b: mode number from the second profile, default: 0
    :param str simulation_name_b: simulation name for the second mode set, default: 'emode'

.. data:: mode_order

    Calculate mode ordering between two mode lists. The result is returned as a list.

    :param profile_a: label of first profile, default: ''
    :type profile_a: str or int
    :param profile_b: label of second profile, default: ''
    :type profile_b: str or int
    :param bool raw_fields: use the raw (un-normalized) field data for the ordering comparison instead of the interpolated fields, default: False
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: scattering

    Calculates the scattering loss from a specified shape and mode using the Volume Current Method [1]. Results are saved in the variables ``SHAPE.metadata['scattering_vertical_edges']`` (total loss from all vertical interfaces), ``SHAPE.metadata['scattering_horizontal_edges']`` (total loss from all horizontal interfaces), ``SHAPE.metadata['scattering_sum']`` (total scattering loss), ``SHAPE.metadata['edges']`` (list of edge points for calculating scattering loss), and ``SHAPE.metadata['scattering_all_edges']`` (scattering loss from corresponding edges). The fields are interpolated to the exact edge position along the interface. The scattering results are also returned by this function as a dictionary keyed by shape name. For a multi-wavelength profile, the return value is a dict keyed by wavelength.

    [1] T. Barwicz and H. A. Haus, "Three-dimensional analysis of scattering losses due to sidewall roughness in microphotonic waveguides," J. Lightwave Technol. 23, 2719 (2005).

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param str shape: name of the shape for calculating the interfacial scattering, can also be a list of shapes or None (which calculates scattering for all shapes), default: None
    :param str shapes: alias for shape
    :param mode_list: mode number, list of mode numbers, or 'all', default: 'all'
    :type mode: int, list, or str
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name for the second mode set, default: 'emode'

.. data:: plot

    Interactive plot for the fields (if available), refractive index, and shapes, or saving a plot. Colorbars are in V/nm for the electric fields, A/nm for the magnetic fields, and W/nm for the Poynting vectors.

    For EME plots in the 'z-x' or 'z-y' planes, the data dropdown also offers an 'Outline' view that displays a geometry-only outline of the declared sections. Once sections are declared with ``straight_section()``, ``pwd_section()``, ``taper_section()``, ``bend_section()`` or ``gds_section()``, calling ``plot()`` before running ``EME()`` shows only the 'Outline' view, which is useful to check the section layout before solving. After ``EME()`` has run, 'Outline' is available alongside the field components.

    A plot of a :math:`\chi^{(2)}` section uses the declared ``excitation`` rather than a unit mode, because conversion depends on power. Each slice is drawn from the forward amplitudes recorded along it, so the generated wavelength builds along the guide instead of stepping at slice boundaries. Without a declared excitation the field shown is the small-signal response, and the solver says so.

    :param component: field component or index, 'Ex/y/z', 'Hx/y/z', 'Sx/y/z', 'Index' or 'Shapes', default: None ('Ex', or 'Index' for a circuit with a closed loop)
    :type component: str or None
    :param str plot_function: plotting function, one of 'real', 'imag', 'abs', 'abs^2' or 'log', default: 'real'
    :param int mode: mode number, default: 0
    :param aspect_ratio: the height:width aspect ratio, 'norm' uses the normal aspect ratio of 0.707, 'real' uses the real aspect ratio defined by the simulation window, or a float specifies the aspect ratio, default: 'norm'
    :type aspect_ratio: str or float
    :param bool index_outline: setting index outline, default: True
    :param bool text_display: setting text display, default: True
    :param bool mesh_display: setting mesh display: the finite-difference grid for an FDM solve, or the triangle mesh for an FEM solve (in the cross-section view), default: False
    :param bool window_display: setting window display, default: False
    :param bool legend: setting inclusion of a legend on the index and shape plots, default: True
    :param port: (EME) the input port that the field is excited from, either a port index or a port name (see :class:`Port`), default: 0
    :type port: int or str
    :param str plane: (EME) plot cross-section plane setting. For 2D simulations, this defaults to 'x-y'. For 3D simulations, it accepts 'x-y', 'z-x', or 'z-y'. The 'z-y' panel also draws the plane of each :data:`monitor`, default: 'z-x'
    :param slice_position: (EME) location of the third dimension for a cross-section display. For example, if `plane` is 'z-x', then the `slice_position` refers to the y-position of the cross-section. If None, it reduces the third dimension with the reduction selected in the plot window: 'sum' (default), which totals the field across the fixed transverse axis, or 'mean', which averages it, default: None
    :type slice_position: float or None
    :param bool forward_only: (EME) render only the forward-propagating component of the field instead of the total (forward + backward) field. This only changes the display decomposition of the already-solved field and does not re-solve, default: False
    :param float wavelength: (EME) which wavelength's field to render on a multi-wavelength circuit, such as the pump or the second harmonic of a :math:`\chi^{(2)}` section. Default: None, the circuit's first wavelength
    :param resolution: (EME) sample spacing in nm along the propagation axis for the 'z-x'/'z-y' longitudinal panels, where smaller is finer and 'auto' picks a spacing of roughly one sample per horizontal display pixel, default: 'auto'
    :type resolution: float or str
    :param str excitation: (EME) render the field launched by a free-space field declared with :data:`free_space_field`, instead of unit amplitude in ``mode`` at ``port``. It also selects which port the field is viewed at. This is the only API surface for viewing one. In the plot window, the same choice appears in the Mode menu as ``'<name> (free space)'``. Default: None
    :param str view: (EME) what the 'z-x' panel shows, either 'layout' (every section where its connections place it on the chip, bends turning and sections after a turn turned with them, both axes in um) or 'simulation' (the circuit unrolled along its length, as solved), default: 'layout'. The 'Physical space' checkbox in the plot window switches between them. Field components follow the guide on the layout, while 'Index' and 'Shapes' stay unrolled. A circuit with a closed loop (a ring closed with :data:`connect_ports`) has no field reconstruction yet: its 'z-x' panel draws the layout outline only, 'Index' and 'Shapes' show its cross-sections, and asking for a field component raises an error.
    :param str normalization: the field family the color scale is normalized to, 'vector' (the full transverse vector at the excitation plane), 'component' (the plotted component alone) or 'section' (each section of a 'z-x' or 'z-y' panel scaled by its own peak, so a dim section such as a free-space gap stays visible), default: 'vector'
    :param profile: render a stored profile by name instead of the EME section. Once a simulation has declared sections, the plot always follows the section, so this is the only way to view a profile saved by an earlier ``FDM(profile=...)`` call. An unknown name raises an error listing the available profiles, default: None
    :type profile: str or None
    :param str file_name: if specified, forces the function to save a file with the given parameters and will not display the interactive plot, file is saved under a directory called EM_figures, default: None
    :param str file_type: file type for saving a plot, 'pdf' or 'png', default: '' (no extension is added to ``file_name`` unless a file type is given)
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: material_explorer

    Interactive material explorer to plot the refractive indices of all available materials. The default wavelength range in the plot corresponds to the recommended range from the material reference listed below the plot. If wavelengths are specified outside this range, the model will be plotted with a dashed line instead of a solid line. User defined materials are also available.

    :param str file_name: if specified, forces the function to save a file with the given parameters and will not display the interactive plot, file is saved under a directory called EM_figures, default: None
    :param str file_type: file type for saving a plot, 'pdf' or 'png', default: '' (no extension is added to ``file_name`` unless a file type is given)
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'

.. data:: refractive_index

    Returns the refractive index from a material name (retrieved from the internal reference list), a MaterialSpec object, or from a custom refractive index value. Optionally, the material's reference (or citation) may be returned.

    :param material: material name, a MaterialSpec (a rotated crystal returns its 3×3 index tensor), or a float/list for a custom value. For AlGaAs, the fraction of Al relative to Ga is included in the material name separated by a comma, for example: "AlGaAs, 0.2" for a Al_{0.2}Ga_{0.8}As.
    :type material: str, MaterialSpec, float, or list
    :param float wavelength: [nm] wavelength, default: 1550
    :param bool reference: additionally return the citation for the material, default: False
    :return: [n_x, n_y, n_z] or ([n_x, n_y, n_z], reference)

.. data:: permeability

    Returns the relative permeability from a material name (retrieved from the internal reference list), a MaterialSpec object, or from a custom permeability value. Optionally, the material's reference (or citation) may be returned.

    :param material: material name, a MaterialSpec, or a float/list of 3 floats for a custom value
    :type material: str, MaterialSpec, float, or list
    :param float wavelength: [nm] wavelength, default: 1550
    :param bool reference: additionally return the citation for the material, default: False
    :return: [permeability_x, permeability_y, permeability_z] or ([permeability_x, permeability_y, permeability_z], reference)

.. data:: permittivity

    Returns the relative permittivity from a material name (retrieved from the internal reference list), a MaterialSpec object, or from a custom value. For isotropic materials this is a 3-element array, and for fully anisotropic materials, such as a crystal rotated by a MaterialSpec's ``theta``, ``phi`` and ``psi``, it is a 3×3 tensor. Optionally, the material's reference (or citation) may be returned.

    :param material: material name, a MaterialSpec, or a float/list for a custom value
    :type material: str, MaterialSpec, float, or list
    :param float wavelength: [nm] wavelength, default: 1550
    :param bool reference: additionally return the citation for the material, default: False
    :return: [eps_x, eps_y, eps_z], a 3×3 array, or the corresponding tuple with reference

.. data:: d_matrix

    Returns the second-order nonlinear d-matrix of a material. Optionally, the material's reference (or citation) may be returned.

    :param str material: material name
    :param float wavelength: [nm] wavelength, default: 1550
    :param bool reference: additionally return the citation for the material, default: False
    :return: d-matrix with shape (3, 6), or (d-matrix, reference)

.. data:: mesh

    Generalized mesh tool for arbitrary shapes on a rectangular grid. This is called internally by ``FDM`` if it has not already been called by the user. Generates vertices for each shape, the actual refractive index for each shape, arrays to define the center points (``x``, ``y``) of the mesh grid, and the relative permittivity and permeability matrices (``permittivity`` and ``permeability``).

    :param str profile: profile name, default: '_default'
    :param bool run_mesh: whether to actually run the meshing step now, or just mark the profile as prepared for meshing without running it, default: True
    :param bool verbose: control the display of the progress bar, default: True
    :param str simulation_name: simulation name, default: 'emode'



Variable Descriptions
---------------------

Descriptions of the variables stored in a simulation file. Variables are read back with
:data:`get` (or, for grids, fields, shapes and whole profiles, with the typed accessors
:data:`get_grid`, :data:`get_fields`, :data:`get_shape` and :data:`get_profile`). Some
variables have an alias, a copy under an older name kept for compatibility. SHAPE stands
for a shape name and NAME for a profile name. :data:`inspect` lists every name :data:`get`
can read.

How the simulation file is organized
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A simulation file has two levels.

**Top-level variables** describe the file and the EME circuit: ``EMode_simulation_file``,
``file_type``, ``emode_version``, ``materials``, ``profiles``,
``propagation_resolution``, and, once the corresponding functions have run,
``sweep_data``, ``S_matrix`` (through ``get('S_matrix')``), ``response`` and ``sources``.
:data:`inspect` returns their names, followed by the per-profile variables and settings
below. Names beginning with an underscore are internal and may change between versions.

**Profiles** live under the top-level ``profiles`` dictionary, one entry per cross-section.
``'_default'`` is the working profile that :data:`settings`, :data:`shape`, :data:`mesh` and
:data:`FDM` act on unless ``profile=`` is given. :data:`label_profile` saves a copy of it
under a name. :data:`FDM` with ``profile=`` saves its result under a name.
:data:`create_profile_set` groups profiles solved at different wavelengths into one
multi-wavelength profile, in which case per-profile results come back as a dictionary keyed
by wavelength. Every function that reads a profile takes ``profile=NAME``: :data:`get`,
:data:`get_fields`, :data:`get_grid`, :data:`get_shape`, :data:`get_profile`,
:data:`confinement`, :data:`effective_area`, :data:`group_index`, :data:`orthogonality`,
:data:`report`, :data:`scattering`, :data:`mesh`, :data:`FDM`, :data:`delete_profile`,
:data:`reset`, :data:`clear_field_data`. :data:`reset` and :data:`clear_field_data` act on
the profile they are given and leave every other profile alone.

One wavelength of a multi-wavelength profile is ``profile='NAME.WAVELENGTH'``, for example
``get('effective_index', profile='tfln.1550')``. A member can also be named by its own name
(``'NAME.MEMBER'``) when that name is its own, as after :data:`create_profile_set`. A name
that several members share, such as the ``'_default'`` that every member of a labeled
multi-wavelength profile keeps, raises an error naming the ``NAME.WAVELENGTH`` of each.

**Settings** (window, resolution, boundary condition, PML, ...) are part of the profile.
``get(key, profile=NAME)`` returns any of them, under its current name or an older alias,
and ``get_profile(NAME).settings`` returns them all at once.

Per-profile variables
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Read with ``get(key, profile=NAME)`` (default ``NAME='_default'``). A multi-wavelength
profile (a profile set) returns a ``dict[float, ...]`` of the same, keyed by wavelength.

.. glossary::

    background_material
        (*float* or *str*) The background material of the profile's simulation window, setting the default material where no shapes are defined.
